sentences.text: Stenopterygius was an extinct ichthyosaur that lived during the Early to Middle Jurassic in Europe. This medium-sized marine reptile likely possessed a warm-blooded metabolism and a layer of blubber for insulation.
Physically similar to the well-known Ichthyosaurus, it had a smaller skull and narrower flippers. Its skull extended into a long snout and was armed with numerous large teeth.
The species S. quadriscissus and S. triscissus reached a maximum length of about 3.5 meters, while S. uniter could exceed 4 meters in length.
Preserved skin traces revealed that Stenopterygius had countershading, being darker on its back than its belly.
A famous fossil represents a mother and her baby that died during birth, proving that ichthyosaurs were viviparous.
A female Stenopterygius fossil that died in childbirth suggests the species gave birth tail-first, similar to modern whales.
Some Stenopterygius specimens contain fetuses suggesting that head-first birth also occurred.
In 2018, a Stenopterygius specimen was found with evidence of fat similar to that of cetaceans, indicating the animal, and thus all ichthyosaurs, were homeothermic.
The genus Stenopterygius was described by Otto Jaekel in 1904, with the type species being Ichthyosaurus quadriscissus.
Stenopterygius is known from the lectotype GPIT 43/0219-1, a complete skeleton that preserves a very large embryo.
A specimen measuring about 3.15 meters long was found in the Posidonia Shale at Holzmaden, dating to the early Toarcian of the Lower Jurassic, approximately 182 million years ago.
Additional materials were described by Hannah Caine and Michael J. Benton in 2011 from the early Toarcian of Strawberry Bank, Ilminster, England.

Stenopterygius lived in the open sea and hunted fish, cephalopods, and other animals, similar to modern dolphins. It had habits similar to modern dolphins, spending much of its life in open waters hunting fish, cephalopods, and other animals.
Abdominal cavities of Stenopterygius skeletons often contain remains of food. The abdominal cavities of Stenopterygius skeletons frequently contain the remains of its food.
Michael W. Maisch redescribed most of the over 100 known Stenopterygius specimens in 2008. More than 100 known specimens of Stenopterygius were recently redescribed by Michael W. Maisch.
Maisch considered Ichthyosaurus triscissus to be a valid species of Stenopterygius, following Woodward's 1932 work.
Many specimens previously referred to Stenopterygius hauffianus were reassigned to the separate genus Hauffiopteryx.
A new species, Stenopterygius aaleniensis, from the Middle Jurassic of southwest Germany was described in 2012.
Research results indicate that the family Stenopterygiidae is monotypic, including only the type genus Stenopterygius.

Stenopterygius fossils date from the Toarcian to the Aalenian stages. Stenopterygius was an extinct ichthyosaur that lived during the Early to Middle Jurassic (Toarcian to Aalenian) in Europe, including England, France, Germany, Switzerland, and Luxembourg.
The type specimen of Stenopterygius dates to the early Toarcian stage of the Early Jurassic, approximately 182 million years ago.
The time range for Stenopterygius is from the Toarcian to the Aalenian, between 184.2 and 170.9 million years ago.
